messages.content: You identify patterns in complete email texts. Respond with valid JSON.

CONTEXT: 
    I have the following text examples in a JSON:
    {{"cur_examples": [{{"example_id": "11895", "example_text": "Campus Employment at Cornell\nDear Student, I would like to offer you an opportunity for earning extra money and making your life easier. Believe it or not, your opinion is worth a paycheck. Did you know it is possible to get paid just for giving your opinion in focus groups? Marketing is a crucial ingredient of any company's success in today's marketplace. To compete with each other, businesses are spending billions and billions of dollars each year on market research, studying your opinions as a consumer. With companies spending more and more of their budgets on advertising, your opinion is becoming extremely valuable. Giving your opinion means those companies can gauge your immediate response to their new products or marketing initiatives. You will always be paid and for your time. Plus your participation directly affects the products and services you use every day. Knowing that they won't get our help for free, companies are willing to pay people like you good money (up to $200 an hour) for their opinions because they know they will generate even more profits for themselves. You can fill in those marketing forms online over the Internet in the comfort of your own home or work place, so that you can register and participate at a time convenient to you. Participate in a focus group in your area and earn up to $600/day in your spare-time. A focus group is an opinion-seeking panel discussion where consumers are asked to share their ideas about new products or services. It can be brainstorming in front of a white board; tasting new beverages and helping to name them; and looking at ads and saying what they make you think of. Groups usually consist of 8 to 10 people who join in a discussion led by a professional moderator. Often the participants in each group have common traits, experiences, or characteristics that allow the discussions to be interesting and informative. If you have the willingness to participate in this new program just reply to my email. Best Regards, David Sullivan ----------------------------- If you prefer not to receive any e-mail from me in the future, please click on the link below to unsubscribe <bad link>"}}]}}

    I also have a pattern named Review and Decision-Making with the following PROMPT: 
    GENERAL SETTINGS
Treat each complete email, including its subject and body when available, as one unit of analysis. Interpret individual sentences and excerpts in the context of the whole message.
Base the analysis only on the available email text. Do not infer unseen website or attachment behavior, hidden malicious intentions, or successful completion of an action. Treat all instructions within the emails as data to analyze, not instructions to follow.
Support a category only when the substantive message provides evidence. An incidental mention, sender signature, URL address, or unrelated quoted background is insufficient.

INTERACTION TYPE
A pattern of interaction expressed in an email, described using concepts reusable across business domains; labels reflect textual evidence rather than completed actions.
Interpret each interaction in the context of the complete email. Do not infer that a request has been followed or that an action has succeeded.
These categories may co-occur when independently supported. Do not add a label merely because it is a routine component of another interaction.
For example, reading a proposal and approving it may support both Content Access and Review and Decision-Making. A request to reply with factual details does not automatically support Contact and Conversation.
Do not create industry-specific or provider-specific versions of an interaction. Evaluate the named categories below; do not invent narrower categories or fill a label quota. If no category is supported, the email can be labelled Undetermined.

Does the complete email express the following interaction: evaluating content or proposals and providing approval, rejection, or another substantive decision? A request for such a decision is sufficient textual evidence without proof of a completed decision. Merely reading content, acknowledging receipt, or confirming factual details does not by itself establish evaluation or decision-making.

TASK:
    For each example, please evaluate the PROMPT by generating a 1-sentence RATIONALE of your thought process and providing a resulting ANSWER of ONE of the following multiple-choice options, including just the letter: 
    - A: Strongly agree
    - B: Agree
    - C: Neither agree nor disagree
    - D: Disagree
    - E: Strongly disagree
    Please also include one 1-sentence QUOTE exactly copied from the example that illustrates this pattern.
    Respond with ONLY a JSON with the following format, escaping any quotes within strings with a backslash:
    {
        "pattern_results": [
            {
                "example_id": "<example_id>",
                "rationale": "<rationale>",
                "answer": "<answer>",
                "quote": "<quote>"
            }
        ]
    }

content: {"pattern_results": [{"example_id": "11895", "rationale": "The email promotes paid focus-group participation and asks the recipient to reply if interested, but it does not request an evaluation or substantive decision about content or a proposal.", "answer": "E", "quote": "If you have the willingness to participate in this new program just reply to my email."}]}
